title: Steel Frame Skyscraper
body:
Steel Frame Skyscraper is a tall building whose weight is carried by a skeleton of steel columns and beams, with floors hung from that frame and walls that carry no structural load. The type made the modern skyscraper possible, because the frame, not the wall, sets the height limit.

Steel-frame construction rose in Chicago and New York in the late nineteenth century, and it remains the default structure for tall commercial buildings, valued for speed of erection and open, column-spaced floor plates.

title: Reinforced Concrete Tower
body:
Reinforced Concrete Tower is a tall building whose structure is cast concrete strengthened with steel bars, giving great stiffness and fire resistance. Concrete towers carry their loads through walls and cores, and they are common for residential towers where floor-to-floor heights are low and repetition is high.

Concrete high-rise construction matured through the twentieth century and now dominates tall housing worldwide, because it is durable, quiet between floors, and economical at residential scale.

title: Bundled Tube Structure
body:
Bundled Tube Structure is a tall building made of several connected tube frames that act together, so the whole cluster resists wind far better than any single tube. The bundled tube let towers rise past the limits of a single frame, and it is the structure behind some of the tallest buildings ever built.

The bundled tube was developed by structural engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, and its most famous example is the Willis Tower in Chicago, completed in 1973.

title: Diagrid Structure
body:
Diagrid Structure is a tall building whose exterior is a diagonal grid of steel members that carries both gravity and wind loads, removing the need for many interior columns. The diagrid gives a distinctive criss-cross facade and a very efficient use of steel.

Diagrid towers became prominent in the twenty-first century, with examples such as 30 St Mary Axe in London and the Hearst Tower in New York, both celebrated for their structural honesty and open interiors.

title: Outrigger and Belt-Truss System
body:
Outrigger and Belt-Truss System is a tall building in which a central concrete core is linked to perimeter columns by deep outrigger arms at one or more mechanical floors, with belt trusses tying the perimeter together. The system stiffens the tower against wind sway without thickening every floor.

Outriggers are standard practice for supertall towers, because they let a slender tower stay comfortable for occupants high above the street while keeping the core compact.

title: Tube-in-Tube Structure
body:
Tube-in-Tube Structure is a tall building with an outer framed tube and an inner core tube working together, sharing gravity and wind loads between perimeter and core. The outer tube carries much of the wind load, while the core carries services and vertical transport.

Tube-in-tube construction underpinned many late-twentieth-century towers, and it remains a clear, teachable model of how a tall building divides its structural work.

title: Megacolumn and Core System
body:
Megacolumn and Core System is a tall building whose loads are carried by a small number of very large perimeter columns linked to a central core, leaving wide open floors between them. The megacolumns give the tower a bold rhythm on its facade and a flexible interior for offices or hotels.

Megacolumn systems suit mixed-use supertall towers, where large column-free spaces are valuable and the structure itself becomes part of the building's identity.

title: Timber High-Rise
body:
Timber High-Rise is a tall building whose structure is engineered timber — cross-laminated panels and glued-laminated columns and beams — rather than steel or concrete. Timber towers store carbon, assemble quickly from prefabricated parts, and give warm, natural interiors.

Timber high-rise construction is a young but fast-growing type, with completed towers in Europe and North America proving that wood can rise well beyond the traditional low-rise limit.
